chapterTitle: Raised With Christ — Put Off the Old, Put On the New, and Do Everything in His Name
themeTitle: “Your Life Is Hidden With Christ — So Live From Where You Really Are”

scripture.text: If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God.
scripture.understanding: The word εἰ, ‘if’, here means ‘since’: Paul is not doubting that they were raised, he is building on it. συνηγέρθητε, you were raised together, picks up 2:12, where they were raised with Christ through faith. Because that is true, ζητεῖτε, keep seeking, the things ἄνω, above. The present tense means a continual pursuit. And the place is defined by a Person: “where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God.” The right hand is the seat of authority from Psalm 110:1, the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. The Christian life starts with where Jesus is sitting.

scripture.text: Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.
scripture.understanding: Verse 1 says seek; verse 2 says φρονεῖτε, set your mind — direct your thinking, your attitude, your inner orientation. The same verb appears in Philippians 2:5, ‘have this mind in you’. Seeking is the pursuit; setting the mind is the steady thought-life behind it. Paul contrasts the things above with τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, the things on the earth. He does not mean that creation is evil. He means the whole realm of the rules and regulations of chapter 2 and the sins of verses 5–9: everything that belongs to life apart from Christ.

scripture.text: For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
scripture.understanding: Here is the reason: “For you died.” The aorist ἀπεθάνετε points to a completed event — their death with Christ (2:20). And your ζωή, life, κέκρυπται, has been hidden, perfect tense: it was hidden and it remains hidden. Your real life is kept safe with Christ in God, hidden from the world's sight and beyond the reach of any enemy. The false teachers spoke of hidden mysteries; Paul says the most precious hidden thing is your own life, stored with Christ.

scripture.text: When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory.
scripture.understanding: What is hidden will not stay hidden. When Christ is φανερωθῇ, revealed, made visible — at His return — you will also be revealed with Him ἐν δόξῃ, in glory. Notice the title: “Christ, our life.” Christ is not only the giver of life; He is the life. Our future is tied to His appearing. Today the world does not see who believers really are; on that day it will. As John says, “when he is revealed, we will be like him” (1 John 3:2).

scripture.text: Put to death therefore your members which are on the earth: sexual immorality, uncleanness, depraved passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry;
scripture.understanding: Now the practical consequence: νεκρώσατε, put to death. The aorist imperative calls for decisive action. You died with Christ (v. 3); now treat sin as something already dead. Your μέλη, members, “which are on the earth” means your earthly ways of using the body. Then comes a list moving from outward acts to inner desires: πορνεία, sexual immorality; ἀκαθαρσία, uncleanness; πάθος, depraved passion; ἐπιθυμία κακή, evil desire; and πλεονεξία, covetousness — literally ‘wanting more’. Paul calls covetousness εἰδωλολατρία, idolatry, because whatever you crave above God becomes your god.

scripture.text: for which things’ sake the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience.
scripture.understanding: These are not small matters. Because of them “the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience.” ὀργή is God's settled, holy opposition to evil, not a sudden temper. The present tense ‘comes’ means it is coming and certain. The phrase ‘sons of disobedience’ (υἱοὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας) is a Hebrew idiom: people whose character is defined by disobedience. Believers are not under that wrath, but they must not make peace with the things that bring it.

scripture.text: You also once walked in those, when you lived in them;
scripture.understanding: Paul is honest about their past: “You also once walked in those, when you lived in them.” περιεπατήσατε, you walked, is Paul's word for a pattern of life. ἐζῆτε, you lived, describes the atmosphere they breathed. This is not shame-mongering; it is a reminder of how far grace has brought them. ‘Once’ marks a boundary. That was then.

scripture.text: but now you also put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and shameful speaking out of your mouth.
scripture.understanding: “But now” — the turning point of the gospel. ἀπόθεσθε, put away, is the word for taking off clothing. Lay these aside like filthy garments. The second list moves to sins of temper and tongue: ὀργή, anger (settled anger); θυμός, wrath (a sudden outburst); κακία, malice, ill will that wants harm for others; βλασφημία, slander, speech that tears people down; and αἰσχρολογία, shameful speaking, foul and abusive talk “out of your mouth.” The list ends at the mouth, because the heart overflows there.

scripture.text: Don’t lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old man with his doings,
scripture.understanding: μὴ ψεύδεσθε, “Don’t lie to one another.” Lying destroys the fellowship of a body (compare Ephesians 4:25: “we are members of one another”). The reason given is clothing language: ἀπεκδυσάμενοι, having stripped off, the παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον, the old man, “with his doings” (πράξεσιν, practices). The ‘old man’ is who you were in Adam, before Christ. That person was crucified with Christ (Romans 6:6). Lying belongs to his wardrobe, not yours.

scripture.text: and have put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator,
scripture.understanding: And you have ἐνδυσάμενοι, put on, τὸν νέον, the new man. The new self is not finished: it is ἀνακαινούμενον, being renewed, present tense, continually made new, εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν, into full knowledge. The pattern is “the image of his Creator” — an echo of Genesis 1, where humanity was made in God's image. Sin defaced that image; in Christ, who is “the image of the invisible God” (1:15), it is being restored. Sanctification is God re-creating you to look like Jesus.

scripture.text: where there can’t be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, freeman; but Christ is all, and in all.
scripture.understanding: In this new humanity the old walls fall. Ἕλλην and Ἰουδαῖος, Greek and Jew, the great religious divide; περιτομή and ἀκροβυστία, circumcision and uncircumcision, the ritual divide the false teachers stressed (2:11); βάρβαρος, barbarian, anyone who did not speak Greek; Σκύθης, Scythian, whom the ancient world regarded as the most savage of all; δοῦλος and ἐλεύθερος, bondservant and freeman, the social divide. None of these define the believer, because “Christ is all, and in all.” He is everything that matters, and He lives in every one of them.

scripture.text: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
scripture.understanding: Now the new wardrobe. Put on “therefore” — because of who you are. Three titles, all once used of Israel, now given to believers: ἐκλεκτοί, chosen; ἅγιοι, holy; ἠγαπημένοι, beloved (perfect tense: loved and still loved). Identity comes first; behaviour follows. Then five garments: σπλάγχνα οἰκτιρμοῦ, a heart of compassion (literally ‘bowels of mercy’, deep gut-level pity); χρηστότης, kindness; ταπεινοφροσύνη, lowliness; πραΰτης, humility or gentleness; and μακροθυμία, perseverance, being long-tempered rather than short-tempered. Every one of them is a quality of Jesus Himself.

scripture.text: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
scripture.understanding: ἀνεχόμενοι, “bearing with one another” — putting up with people's weaknesses and irritating habits. χαριζόμενοι, forgiving — a word built on χάρις, grace: forgiveness is grace given freely. “If any man has a complaint” (μομφή, a cause for blame) — Paul assumes Christians will have real grievances. The standard is not how sorry the person is or how small the offence is, but how Christ treated you: “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.” The forgiven forgive.

scripture.text: Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
scripture.understanding: “Above all these things” — over all the other garments, like an outer belt or coat — put on ἀγάπη, love. Love is σύνδεσμος, the bond, the ligament that ties everything together (the same word used of the body's ligaments in 2:19). Without love the virtues fall apart; with love they become τελειότης, perfection, completeness, maturity. The false teachers offered perfection through knowledge; Paul says it comes through love.

scripture.text: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body; and be thankful.
scripture.understanding: “Let the peace of God rule in your hearts” — the best manuscripts read ‘peace of Christ’. βραβευέτω means to act as umpire, the referee at the games who decides the outcome. When you face a decision or a conflict, let Christ's peace make the call. This is peace “to which also you were called in one body,” so it is a peace between believers, not only within one. And then a short command: εὐχάριστοι γίνεσθε, “be thankful.” Gratitude is the soil in which peace grows.

scripture.text: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.
scripture.understanding: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.” ἐνοικείτω means to take up residence, to live at home. Christ's word is not to be a guest you visit on Sundays; it should live in your house, πλουσίως, richly, abundantly. When it does, the church becomes a teaching community: διδάσκοντες, teaching, and νουθετοῦντες, admonishing, warning one another. And it becomes a singing community: ψαλμοί, psalms; ὕμνοι, hymns of praise; ᾠδαὶ πνευματικαί, spiritual songs. ᾄδοντες, singing, “with grace in your heart to the Lord.” The word of Christ fills the church with both instruction and song.

scripture.text: Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father, through him.
scripture.understanding: The summary of the whole section: “Whatever you do, in word or in deed” — λόγῳ ἢ ἔργῳ, everything said and everything done. Do it all ἐν ὀνόματι, in the name of the Lord Jesus — as His representative, by His authority, for His reputation. Paul does not divide life into sacred and secular. Washing dishes, writing a report, speaking to a neighbour can all be done in His name. And again, gratitude: εὐχαριστοῦντες, giving thanks to God the Father through Him. Thanksgiving is mentioned three times in verses 15–17.

scripture.text: Wives, be in subjection to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
scripture.understanding: Now Paul applies the new life to the household, in a pattern called a ‘household code’. Unlike the codes of Greek philosophers, which spoke only to the man in charge, Paul addresses every member directly, as a moral person. γυναῖκες, wives; ὑποτάσσεσθε, be in subjection — a voluntary arranging of oneself under, the same word used of Christ submitting to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:28). The qualifier transforms it: “as is fitting in the Lord.” ἀνῆκεν, fitting, proper. This is submission inside a relationship with Christ, never submission to sin.

scripture.text: Husbands, love your wives, and don’t be bitter against them.
scripture.understanding: ἄνδρες, husbands: ἀγαπᾶτε, love your wives. In a culture where a husband had legal power over his wife, Paul commands not authority but ἀγάπη, self-giving love. And he adds a specific prohibition: μὴ πικραίνεσθε, “don’t be bitter against them.” πικραίνω means to make bitter or to be embittered — harsh, resentful, sour. A husband's love is tested in the small irritations of daily life.

scripture.text: Children, obey your parents in all things, for this pleases the Lord.
scripture.understanding: τέκνα, children, are addressed as members of the church who would hear this letter read aloud. ὑπακούετε, obey — literally ‘hear under’, listen and respond. The reason: “for this pleases the Lord” (εὐάρεστον, well-pleasing). Children's obedience is not only good manners; it is worship. Even the youngest believer can please the Lord.

scripture.text: Fathers, don’t provoke your children, so that they won’t be discouraged.
scripture.understanding: πατέρες, fathers, μὴ ἐρεθίζετε, don't provoke, stir up, exasperate your children. Constant criticism, unfair demands, harshness and favouritism all provoke. The result is that they ἀθυμῶσιν, lose heart, become spiritless and discouraged. Roman fathers had near-absolute power over their children; Paul limits that power by the child's heart. Parental authority exists to build children up, not to crush them.

scripture.text: Servants, obey in all things those who are your masters according to the flesh, not just when they are looking, as men pleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing God.
scripture.understanding: The longest instruction goes to δοῦλοι, servants or slaves, who made up a large part of the early church. Onesimus, a runaway slave from Colossae, was travelling with this letter (4:9). Obey your earthly κύριοι, masters, “not just when they are looking” — ὀφθαλμοδουλία, ‘eye-service’, working only when watched; “as men pleasers” — ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι, people who live for human approval. Instead, ἐν ἁπλότητι καρδίας, “in singleness of heart,” undivided sincerity, φοβούμενοι τὸν κύριον, fearing the Lord. The real Master is always watching.

scripture.text: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men,
scripture.understanding: “And whatever you do, work heartily” — ἐκ ψυχῆς ἐργάζεσθε, literally ‘work from the soul’. Put your whole self into it. “As for the Lord, and not for men.” This one sentence turned the ancient world's view of labour upside down. The lowest task became an offering to Christ. No work is too humble when it is done for Him.

scripture.text: knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.
scripture.understanding: The motive is future: ἀπολήμψεσθε, you will receive in full, from the Lord τὴν ἀνταπόδοσιν, the repayment, “of the inheritance.” This is remarkable, because under Roman law a slave could not inherit anything. Yet Paul tells these slaves that they are heirs. Then the key line: τῷ κυρίῳ Χριστῷ δουλεύετε, “you serve the Lord Christ.” Their true employer is Jesus.

scripture.text: But he who does wrong will receive again for the wrong that he has done, and there is no partiality.
scripture.understanding: “But he who does wrong (ἀδικῶν) will receive again (κομίσεται) for the wrong that he has done.” Justice cuts both ways. A slave who cheats will answer for it — and so will a master who abuses (see 4:1). “And there is no partiality” — προσωπολημψία, literally ‘receiving the face’, judging by appearance or status. Before God, the master's rank gives no protection and the slave's low position is no excuse. Everyone stands before the same just Judge.

visualMeditations.title: The Life in the Vault
visualMeditations.image: Picture a deep vault, sealed and guarded, in the throne room of heaven. Inside it lies a single treasure, kept safe: your life. Not the life the world sees — your job, your reputation, your struggles, your age — but your true life, the person God made you to be in Christ. The door of the vault has two names written on it: Christ, and God. Nothing on earth can break in. No accuser, no illness, no failure, no death can reach what is inside. Now picture the day the vault opens. Christ steps out into the sight of all creation, and as He is revealed, you are revealed with Him — the hidden life finally visible, shining with His glory.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul says “your life is hidden with Christ in God” (v. 3). Hidden means two things: kept safe, and not yet seen. Your real identity is not on display yet. People may misunderstand you, circumstances may hide it, and even you may struggle to see it. But it is secure, because it is held inside the relationship between the Father and the Son. And it will not stay hidden for ever: “When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory” (v. 4). The believer lives now from a secure, hidden place, and looks forward to a glorious unveiling.

visualMeditations.title: The Changing Room
visualMeditations.image: Picture a person entering a changing room wearing filthy, torn clothes that still smell of the grave: anger, malice, slander, lies, foul speech. One by one the garments come off and are thrown out — they no longer fit, they belong to someone who died. Hanging on the wall is a new set of clothes, cut to the measure of Christ Himself: compassion, kindness, lowliness, gentleness, patience. The person puts them on one at a time. Then, over everything, comes a final garment — a broad belt of love that ties the whole outfit together so that nothing slips. The person steps out looking strangely like Jesus.
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul uses clothing language throughout this chapter: “put them all away” (v. 8), “you have put off the old man” (v. 9), “have put on the new man” (v. 10), “Put on therefore” (v. 12), and “Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection” (v. 14). Changing your character is not mainly about effort to improve the old clothes; it is about taking off what belongs to the dead self and putting on what belongs to the new self. This happened decisively when you came to Christ, and you live it out daily, choice by choice. And love is the belt: without it, every other virtue comes loose.

visualMeditations.title: The Umpire's Whistle
visualMeditations.image: Picture a busy stadium in an ancient city. Two athletes are disputing a result; the crowd is shouting, the competitors are angry, and everyone has an opinion. Then the umpire steps forward, raises his hand and gives his decision, and the matter is settled. Now picture your own heart as that stadium: anxious thoughts, competing voices, hurt feelings, a decision you do not know how to make, a quarrel with a fellow believer. In the middle stands the peace of Christ, holding the authority to make the call. When His peace is present, you go forward; when it is disturbed, you stop and listen.
visualMeditations.meaning: The verb in verse 15 is βραβεύω, to act as umpire. Paul says, “let the peace of God rule in your hearts.” Christ's peace is meant to be the deciding voice in the life of the believer and of the church. It does not replace Scripture or wisdom, but it guards both. When an action or attitude disturbs the peace Christ gives — and especially the peace of the body “to which also you were called in one body” — that is a signal to stop. Paul immediately adds “and be thankful,” because a grateful heart is the easiest place for Christ's peace to rule.

structure.label: Seek the Things Above (v. 1-4)
structure.body: Because believers were raised with Christ, they must seek and set their minds on the things above, where Christ is enthroned; they died, their life is hidden with Christ in God, and when Christ appears they will appear with Him in glory.

structure.label: Put to Death and Put Away (v. 5-11)
structure.body: Put to death earthly sins of desire and covetousness, which bring God's wrath; put away sins of temper and tongue, and stop lying, because the old man has been put off and the new man put on — a new humanity being renewed in the image of its Creator, where every human division gives way to Christ who is all and in all.

structure.label: Put On the New Wardrobe (v. 12-14)
structure.body: As God's chosen, holy and beloved people, put on compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility and patience; bear with one another and forgive as Christ forgave; and over all of them put on love, the bond of perfection.

structure.label: Peace, Word and Thanksgiving (v. 15-17)
structure.body: Let Christ's peace rule as umpire, let His word dwell richly in the church through teaching and singing, and do everything in word or deed in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to the Father.

structure.label: The New Life at Home and Work (v. 18-25)
structure.body: Wives, husbands, children, fathers and servants are each addressed directly: submission, love without bitterness, obedience, fathers not discouraging children, and wholehearted work done for the Lord, who rewards and judges without partiality.

sections.heading: From Doctrine to Life: Where Christ Is
paragraphs: Colossians 3 is the hinge of the letter. Chapters 1 and 2 have shown who Christ is — the image of the invisible God, the Creator, the Head of the church, the One in whom all fullness dwells, the conqueror of the powers. Now Paul shows what this means for the way believers live. But notice how he begins. He does not start with a rule; he starts with a fact: “If then you were raised together with Christ” (v. 1). In chapter 2, the false teachers offered rules: “don’t handle, nor taste, nor touch” (2:21). Paul said those rules “aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh” (2:23). Here is the alternative. The power to live a holy life does not come from regulations; it comes from union with Christ in His death and resurrection.

Paul gives two commands built on that fact: “seek the things that are above” (v. 1) and “Set your mind on the things that are above” (v. 2). This is not escapism. Heavenly-minded Christians are not useless on earth; as the rest of the chapter shows, they make better spouses, parents and workers. ‘The things above’ are defined by Christ's presence: “where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God” (v. 1). To seek the things above is to orient everything — your desires, decisions, values and hopes — around the enthroned Jesus. As Jesus said, “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

Then come the reasons. “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (v. 3). Your old life ended at the cross. Your new life is secure and, for now, unseen. And it has a future: “When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory” (v. 4). The Christian lives between two events — the resurrection of Christ, in which they already share, and the return of Christ, when their hidden life will be displayed. That is the frame for everything else in the chapter.

sections.heading: Putting Off and Putting On
paragraphs: Because you died with Christ, Paul says, “Put to death therefore your members which are on the earth” (v. 5). There seems to be a contradiction: if I died, why must I put anything to death? The answer is that Paul always moves from what is true in Christ to what must become true in practice. You died to sin's rule; now you must treat sin's desires as the leftovers of a dead life and refuse to feed them. The first list moves inward, from sexual immorality to the evil desire behind it, and ends with “covetousness, which is idolatry” (v. 5). Greed is idolatry because it puts something in God's place as the source of satisfaction and security.

The second list is about the sins of community: “anger, wrath, malice, slander, and shameful speaking out of your mouth” (v. 8), and then lying (v. 9). These are the sins that destroy a church from the inside. Paul's reason is again identity: “you have put off the old man with his doings, and have put on the new man” (vv. 9–10). And the new man is not a finished product but a process: “being renewed in knowledge after the image of his Creator” (v. 10). God is restoring in you the image He intended in Eden, and the pattern is Christ, the true image of God (1:15).

This renewed humanity has no room for the old divisions: “where there can’t be Greek and Jew, circumcision and uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, bondservant, freeman; but Christ is all, and in all” (v. 11). Paul lists the deepest racial, religious, cultural and social barriers of his world and declares them all irrelevant to standing in Christ. Then he shows the new wardrobe: “Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance” (v. 12). Every item is relational, and every item is a description of Jesus. The new self is not a new set of rules; it is Christ's own character being formed in His people, held together by love, “the bond of perfection” (v. 14).

sections.heading: Everything in His Name, Even at Home
paragraphs: Verses 15–17 describe the church as it lives together under Christ. Three things fill it. First, peace: “let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body” (v. 15). Second, the word: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (v. 16), so that believers teach and admonish one another and sing together. Third, thanksgiving, which appears in each verse: “be thankful” (v. 15), “with grace in your heart” (v. 16), “giving thanks to God the Father, through him” (v. 17). The great summary is verse 17: “Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus.” That sentence leaves no part of life outside Christ's lordship.

And so Paul goes straight into the home. The household codes of verses 18–4:1 can sound foreign to modern readers, and some have misused them. But read in their world they are radical. Paul addresses wives, children and slaves directly, as moral persons responsible before the Lord — not as property. Every instruction to the person with less power is matched by an instruction to the person with more: wives and husbands, children and fathers, servants and masters. And the husband's duty is not ‘rule your wife’ but “love your wives, and don’t be bitter against them” (v. 19). The father's duty is not ‘control your children’ but “don’t provoke your children, so that they won’t be discouraged” (v. 21).

The longest section is for servants, and it is full of dignity. Slaves were told to work “in singleness of heart, fearing God” (v. 22), and then: “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men” (v. 23). Then the astonishing promise: “knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ” (v. 24). People with no legal rights to inherit are told that they are heirs of God. And the warning of verse 25 — “there is no partiality” — reaches both ways, as 4:1 makes clear. In Christ, every task becomes worship, and every person, from the slave to the master, answers to the same Lord.

ntConnection.heading: The Twin Letter: Colossians and Ephesians
paragraphs: Colossians 3 has a close twin in Ephesians 4–6, which Paul wrote at about the same time and sent with the same messenger, Tychicus. The ‘put off, put on’ language appears there too: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man, that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit” (Ephesians 4:22), and “put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:24). And the command to forgive is almost identical: “forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32).

There is one striking difference. In Colossians, Paul says, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (v. 16), and the result is psalms, hymns and spiritual songs. In Ephesians, he says, “be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18), and the result is the same: “speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing, and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19). Being filled with the Spirit and being filled with the word of Christ produce the same fruit. The Spirit fills us through the word, and the word comes alive by the Spirit. The two cannot be separated.

The death-and-resurrection pattern of verses 1–4 is the same one Paul teaches in Romans 6: “We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). And the conclusion is the same: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:11). Galatians puts it personally: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I that live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Colossians 3 adds the future horizon: our hidden life will be revealed when Christ appears.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “to conceal (properly, by covering).” The perfect tense κέκρυπται means ‘has been hidden and remains hidden’. The same root gives us ‘cryptic’ and ‘crypt’. In 2:3 Paul used the related word ἀπόκρυφοι for the treasures of wisdom hidden in Christ. Now he says your own life is hidden in the same place. To be hidden is to be safe: like treasure locked in a vault, your life cannot be stolen. It is also to be unseen: the world, and sometimes even you, cannot fully see who you are in Christ. One day the hiding will end in revealing (v. 4).

Strong's: “to deaden, i.e. (figuratively) to subdue.” The word is related to νεκρός, dead, from which we get ‘necro-’ words. Paul uses it in Romans 4:19 of Abraham's body being ‘as good as dead’. Here it is an aorist imperative: a decisive act. The believer does not negotiate with sin or manage it; they treat it as a corpse. This is not self-hatred or physical punishment, which Paul rejected in 2:23. It is refusing, by the power of the risen life, to give earthly desires any more room to live.

Strong's: “to renovate.” The word combines ἀνά, again, and καινός, new in quality. The present participle ἀνακαινούμενον means ‘being continually renewed’. The same word appears in 2 Corinthians 4:16, where the inner person is renewed day by day. The new self is real from the moment of conversion, yet it is still being renovated, like a house restored room by room. The goal is “the image of his Creator” — God remaking you to look like Jesus. Growth is not you becoming a better version of the old self; it is God finishing the new one.

Strong's: “to arbitrate, i.e. (genitive case) to govern (figuratively, prevail).” The word comes from βραβεύς, the umpire at the athletic games, and is related to βραβεῖον, the prize (Philippians 3:14). In 2:18 Paul used a compound of the same word: καταβραβευέτω, ‘let no one disqualify you’ — the false teachers wanted to be the umpires of the Colossians' spiritual lives. Here Paul says the true umpire is Christ's peace. Not human judges, but His peace decides whether you are on course.

Strong's: “to inhabit (figuratively).” The word combines ἐν, in, and οἰκέω, to dwell in a house (οἶκος). It is used of the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers (Romans 8:11; 2 Timothy 1:14) and of faith dwelling in Timothy's family (2 Timothy 1:5). Paul wants the word of Christ to live in the church as in its own home, not as a visitor. And it is to dwell πλουσίως, richly — filling every room, overflowing into conversation and song. A church where the word dwells richly will teach, warn, comfort and sing.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: where your mind lives, what you are still wearing, and who you are really working for.

items.title: Where Is Your Mind?
items.body: The Spirit asks you a simple question: what do you think about when you are not forced to think about anything? Paul says, “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (v. 2). Your thought-life follows your treasure. If your mind keeps returning to money, status, a grievance, a fear or a desire, the Spirit is showing you what has taken the throne. He does not condemn you for it; He invites you to lift your eyes to the One “seated on the right hand of God” (v. 1). Every time your mind drifts, bring it back to Jesus. That is not escape from life; it is the beginning of a new one.

items.title: Old Clothes in the Wardrobe
items.body: Some believers have put off the old self in principle but still keep a few old garments in the wardrobe, just in case: a familiar anger, a habit of slander, a small lie that makes life easier, a secret desire. The Spirit is gently opening that wardrobe. “But now you also put them all away” (v. 8) — all of them. He knows which garment you reach for under pressure. Let Him name it today, and give it up. Then let Him clothe you with what belongs to Christ: compassion, kindness, lowliness, gentleness and patience, and over all of it, love.

items.title: You Serve the Lord Christ
items.body: Many believers feel their daily work is unspiritual — a job they endure between the things that really matter. The Spirit wants to change that. “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men” (v. 23). Your boss is not your final audience; your customers, your family, even your church leaders are not your final audience. “You serve the Lord Christ” (v. 24). When you are overlooked, underpaid or unthanked, He sees. When no one is watching, He is. Let the Spirit turn your ordinary work into worship, and your workplace into a place where Christ is served.

audit.title: The Mind Check
audit.body: For one day, notice where your mind goes when it is free — in the shower, in traffic, before sleep. Write down the three things it returns to most. Then ask: are these things above or things on the earth? Choose one verse about Christ's reign (v. 1) to bring your mind back each time it drifts.

audit.title: The Wardrobe Check
audit.body: Read the lists in verses 5, 8 and 9 slowly. Circle the one sin that you most often ‘wear’ under pressure. Then read verse 12 and circle the garment that is its opposite. Ask God to help you take off the first and put on the second this week, in one specific relationship.

audit.title: The Forgiveness Check
audit.body: Is there someone you have a complaint against (v. 13)? Write their name down. Then write next to it what Christ has forgiven you. Ask whether you are measuring their debt by your own standard or by His. Decide today to forgive, even if reconciliation takes longer.

practices.title: The Word at Home
practices.body: Take verse 16 literally this week: let the word of Christ dwell in your home. Choose one short passage — Colossians 3:1–4 or 3:12–17 is ideal — and read it aloud each day with your household or, if you live alone, with a friend by phone. Talk about one phrase. Sing a hymn or worship song that carries its message. Let the word become part of the conversation of your home, not just of your Sunday. At the end of the week, write down how it changed the atmosphere and the way you spoke to each other.

practices.title: The ‘In His Name’ Day
practices.body: Pick one ordinary working day and treat every task as done “in the name of the Lord Jesus” (v. 17). Before each piece of work, pause for a few seconds and say, ‘Lord, this is for You.’ Work with the same care whether or not anyone is watching (v. 22). Give thanks at each meal and each finished task. In the evening, write down what was different: your attitude, your quality of work, your patience with others. Repeat it until it stops being an experiment and becomes your way of life.

prayerReflection: “Lord Jesus, You are seated at the right hand of God, and I have been raised with You. Lift my eyes from the things on the earth and set my mind on the things above, where You are. Thank You that I died with You and that my life is hidden with You in God, safe beyond the reach of every enemy. When You appear, I will appear with You in glory; let that hope shape how I live today. By Your power I put to death what belongs to my old life: impurity, evil desire and the greed that is idolatry. I put away anger, malice, slander and every lie. Clothe me with the new self, renewed after Your image. Make me compassionate, kind, humble, gentle and patient. Teach me to bear with others and to forgive as You forgave me. Over everything, wrap me in love. Let Your peace rule in my heart and in Your church, let Your word dwell in me richly, and fill my mouth with thanksgiving and song. In my home, make me loving and not bitter. In my work, let me serve You heartily, knowing that I serve the Lord Christ. Whatever I do, in word or deed, let me do it all in Your name, giving thanks to the Father through You. Amen.”

storyConnections.title: The Servant Who Would Not Forgive
storyConnections.summary: Peter asked Jesus how often he should forgive a brother who sinned against him — up to seven times? Jesus said, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22), and told a story. A king settled accounts with a servant who owed him ten thousand talents, a debt no one could ever repay. When the servant begged for patience, the king was “moved with compassion, released him, and forgave him the debt” (Matthew 18:27). But that same servant went out, found a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii, seized him by the throat and threw him into prison. The king called him back and said, “Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?” (Matthew 18:33). The parable is the story behind Paul's words, “even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” (v. 13). Those who have been forgiven an unpayable debt cannot hold small debts over others.

storyConnections.title: Singing at Midnight in Philippi
storyConnections.summary: In Philippi, Paul and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods and thrown into the inner prison with their feet in the stocks. Their circumstances gave them every reason for bitterness. Instead, “about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them” (Acts 16:25). An earthquake opened the doors and loosened every chain. The terrified jailer was about to kill himself, but Paul stopped him, and that night the jailer and his household believed and were baptized. This is Colossians 3:15–17 lived out: the peace of Christ ruling in a dark place, the word of Christ overflowing in song, and thanksgiving that does not depend on circumstances. The prisoners listened, and a household was saved.

storyConnections.title: Joseph in Potiphar's House
storyConnections.summary: Joseph was sold by his brothers and bought as a slave by Potiphar, an Egyptian officer. He had every reason to do the minimum. Instead, he worked so faithfully that the Lord was with him and blessed Potiphar's house for his sake, and Potiphar put everything he owned in Joseph's care. When Potiphar's wife tried to seduce him day after day, Joseph refused: how could he do this great wickedness and sin against God? He was falsely accused and thrown into prison, yet even there the Lord was with him, and the jailer trusted him with everything. Joseph worked in singleness of heart, fearing God, whether anyone was watching or not. Centuries before Paul wrote it, Joseph lived out the truth of verse 23: work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men. His real Master saw, and in time lifted him to the right hand of Pharaoh.
